messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: branches, versions, and maintenance
parts:
Ben brought up the issue of branching
our code and what goes into which branch:

We also probably need a branch called v1.0.x or v1.x. And a set of
guidelines for what goes in what branch. And to write down our
accumulated set of guidelines so that other people can find them.

Below is what I think. Anyone else have an opinion?

Given our limited resources, my thinking was that we would
NOT support anything other than the currently distributed
version. That means we tag the releases for laughs, but
don't maintain them going forward.

In particular, I want to respond to users who say they're
using an old version by first telling them to upgrade,
then report bugs.

I don't even care if we distribute older versions. We
can leave them on Google Code and deprecate them, but I
don't want people following links to older versions when
newer versions are available.

Within minor versions, when going from 1.x.y to 1.x.(y+1),
there's no reason to support 1.x.y going forward.

It's more of an issue when we change functionality, as in
going from 1.0.y to 1.1.0. But as long as we don't break
backward compatibility, there shouldn't be a problem for users
in supporting just the newer versions.

When we change major versions AND they break backward
compatibility, say going from 1.1.x to 2.0.0, it may be
worth taking up this discussion again.

For commercial customers, things are different. They often
don't want to upgrade even minor versions of software that
works as it is. Or they weren't sold a license that lets
them upgrade. Given that we're not selling Stan, I don't
see that as an issue, either.

What bigger companies do for commercial software (e.g.,
MS for Windows or Office, Oracle for Java) is support some older
versions, then eventually retire them so that support doesn't
drag on forever. Apple's very agressive at retiring old version
support compared to MS.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: branches, versions, and maintenance
parts:
On Wednesday, September 5, 2012 5:10:08 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Given our limited resources, my thinking was that we would
NOT support anything other than the currently distributed
version.  That means we tag the releases for laughs, but
don't maintain them going forward.

I agree that our preference is for users to upgrade to the latest version. But having tagged old releases serves at least two additional purposes. One is to serve as endpoints for a git bisect when something that was previously working is later found to be broken and we don't know why. You can do

git bisect start HEAD v1.2 --      # HEAD is bad, v1.2 is good

to find the commit that caused the problem. This works best when the tag for the working state is recent.

Also, some projects prefer that people branch off the last released version rather than whatever state master is in

git branch feature v1.2

This can make it easier to merge those branches into master later.

It's more of an issue when we change functionality, as in
going from 1.0.y to 1.1.0.  But as long as we don't break
backward compatibility, there shouldn't be a problem for users
in supporting just the newer versions.

When we change major versions AND they break backward
compatibility, say going from 1.1.x to 2.0.0, it may be
worth taking up this discussion again.

We also need a policy as to what the process should be for deciding whether something that goes into master also goes into 1.1.0 and / or 1.0.y . For a lot of projects, the "release manager" is asked on the list to git cherry-pick commit deadbeef from master to whatever branch is waiting to be released. In other projects, people git cherry-pick commit deadbeef to whatever branch they personally feel is appropriate and announce it on the list to see if there are any objections. But we probably don't want to be in a situation where the release manager doesn't know what is going into the release he is managing.

Ben

Ben was suggesting we define what goes into each branch. As a
proposal, how is this for a start?
- Major version: additional functionality (major, whatever that
means), no guarantee on backwards compatibility
- Minor version: additional functionality (minor), backwards compatible
- Patch version: bug fixes, backwards compatible, might include
additional functionality

I would think adding new samplers would increase minor version. Maybe
NUTS3 would increase major version or not. Solving MCMC definitely
increases the major version. Maybe twice. Fixing numeric stability
increases patch version.

> For commercial customers, things are different. They often
> don't want to upgrade even minor versions of software that
> works as it is. Or they weren't sold a license that lets
> them upgrade. Given that we're not selling Stan, I don't
> see that as an issue, either.

I also think this is a non-issue. If a later version fixes the problem
and a user (commercial or non) doesn't want to download a newer
version, I don't think we should prioritize our efforts making fixes
to older versions. If someone volunteers to maintain older versions, I
won't stop them.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: branches, versions, and maintenance
parts:
On Wednesday, September 5, 2012 7:38:15 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Now that I have, I completely agree.  I would
think branching on major versions makes sense.

I don't know how to do it in git, though.
git branch takes an optional start-point, which can be a tag or a hash but defaults to HEAD.

> One is to serve as endpoints for a git bisect when something that was previously working
> is later found to be broken and we don't know why. You can do
>
> git bisect start HEAD v1.2 --      # HEAD is bad, v1.2 is good
>
> to find the commit that caused the problem. This works best when the tag for the working state is recent.

That sounds like a great idea.  Can you not
do it commit by commit?
Doing it one commit at a time would be unefficient. Under a bisection algorithm,
git bisect start HEAD v1.2 --

git bisect good # 1
git bisect bad  #  2
git bisect bad  #  3
...
git bisect good # K

you get approximately halfway to the bad commit at each of the K steps.

> We also need a policy as to what the process should be for deciding whether something that goes into master also goes
> into 1.1.0 and / or 1.0.y .

I'd rather not push backwards.  What's the benefit
of doing that?

Presuming that everything that goes into 1.1.0 or 1.0.y will also go into master (and thus 2.0.0), then you always have to commit to multiple places. Given that, every project that I know of commits to master first so that anyone can git pull origin/master and see the commit(s). And then there is some process by which it is decided whether to also commit it to 1.1.0 or 1.0.y .

> For a lot of projects, the "release manager" is asked on the list to git cherry-pick commit
> deadbeef from master to whatever branch is waiting to be released. In other projects, people git cherry-pick commit
> deadbeef to whatever branch they personally feel is appropriate and announce it on the list to see if there are any
> objections. But we probably don't want to be in a situation where the release manager doesn't know what is going into
> the release he is managing.

Let me digest that (sorry). But first, what's "deadbeef"?
8 symbols of a hypothetical SHA-1 hash. As in "Should we put commit 'deadbeef' into the 1.1.0 branch?"

I'm happy to read external things if there is some
kind of best practices doc going over this kind of
thing.

There are different ways of doing everything. Here is a nice blogpost

https://rwmj.wordpress.com/2010/05/14/git-cherry-pick-wins/

Ben
